messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leilani, a 53-year-old widow who runs a small convenience shop in Honolulu, still cannot piece together the sequence of that afternoon three years ago when her husband, Kimo, collapsed behind the counter. The memory arrives not as a story but as a film: the smell of the beer he had been drinking, the way his eyes went blank, the paramedics’ voices that seemed to come from far away. After the film had played through, Leilani found herself scanning the shop floor with a new vigilance—every bottle in a customer's hand, every distant siren, every glimpse of a blue uniform felt like a threat she had to spot before it struck again. She knows he died of a sudden cardiac event, but if anyone asks her to describe what happened she can only shake her head—the details feel jumbled, the timeline gone. That smell of alcohol now hits her without warning. A customer carrying a six-pack walks through the door and Leilani’s chest tightens, her breath short, as though she is back in that moment. She has learned to brace herself every time the bell rings, scanning for beer bottles or for anyone who might start talking about loss—a casual remark about a relative’s funeral, a customer mentioning they just lost a parent. The mere word “funeral” makes her stomach drop, and she has begun leaving the cash register to her part-time clerk whenever she sees a hearse drive past the shop window.

In the months after Kimo’s death, Leilani found herself unable to relax even in her own living room. She would be sitting on the couch, no danger in sight, and her heart would pound as if she were being chased. These false alarms convinced her that something was fundamentally wrong with her—that she was broken, that her life had been destroyed beyond repair. She started to believe she no longer knew who she was. Without Kimo, her identity as a wife, as half of a couple, felt erased. The thought of a future seemed absurd; she saw only an empty stretch of years ahead. Each time the memory of his face in those final seconds forced itself into her mind—often at night, or when she was alone in the shop after closing—she felt that sense of annihilation all over again. And that hopelessness, in turn, made the intrusions worse: the more she believed her life was over, the more the film replayed.

The cycle tightened gradually. A visit to Kimo’s grave became unbearable; she went once and spent the whole time trembling, certain that grief would swallow her. Now she drives miles out of her way to avoid the cemetery. When a neighbor mentioned her own husband’s passing last month, Leilani made an excuse and walked out of the shop, her hands shaking. The conversation had triggered the film—Kimo’s face, the beer smell—and then the thought crashed in: *This is my life now, ruined.* That belief made her feel even more unsafe, as if the world were a place where loss lurked behind every corner. She began watching customers more warily, looking for signs of sadness or alcohol, trying to predict the next trigger.

The cost of these habits has been real. Her shop’s profits have slipped because she disappears to the back room several times a shift. Her daughter, who lives on the mainland, calls and asks why Leilani sounds so distant; Leilani cannot explain that the mere sound of a sympathetic voice makes her feel like she is drowning. She has stopped attending church, stopped meeting friends for coffee. The only thing that feels safe is her home, but even there the memory finds her.

What finally brought her to a therapist was a morning last week when a delivery driver reeking of beer walked into the store. Leilani froze, then sprinted to the bathroom and locked the door, sobbing. She sat on the floor for twenty minutes, the film playing over and over, the belief that her life was destroyed repeating like a mantra. When she finally emerged, the driver had left his boxes on the counter. She knew then that she could no longer manage this alone. She is terrified that talking about it will make the intrusions worse, but she is more afraid of spending the rest of her years trapped behind that locked door.
